answer.sourceLine: This line is listed among Sun Tzu’s misattributed quotations ↗: it appears nowhere in The Art of War and is only “sometimes erroneously prepended” to its opening line. Its first half restates the ancient Roman maxim Si vis pacem, para bellum (“if you want peace, prepare for war”), traced to the writer Vegetius ↗; the neat “in war prepare for peace” reversal is a modern addition with no identifiable author.

source.excerpt: In peace prepare for war, in war prepare for peace.
trail: Not in The Art of War. Wikiquote files this line under Sun Tzu’s Misattributed quotations ↗, noting it is only “sometimes erroneously prepended” to the book’s real opening line.
A Roman idea, not a Chinese one. Wikiquote identifies the line as “a variation of the Roman motto Si vis pacem, para bellum,” whose documented source is Vegetius’s De re militari ↗.
No early attribution. Per Wikiquote, the phrase’s earliest Google Books appearance is 1920 ↗, in a pharmaceutical journal — and even then it carried no author’s name.
source.excerptNote: Sun Tzu’s Art of War in fact opens: “The art of war is of vital importance to the State.” The line above is a separate modern saying that gets glued onto that opening.
source.rightsNote: The exact double-chiasmus wording has no identifiable author — its earliest known Google Books appearance (1920) carried no attribution — so no copyright status can be asserted for this phrasing. The two works it draws on, Sun Tzu’s Art of War and Vegetius’s Roman maxim, are both ancient and long in the public domain, but that does not attach to this particular modern saying.

author.name: Vegetius
author.kicker: The documented root of the idea
author.heading: Vegetius, and the Roman maxim behind the line
author.metaLine: Late 4th century AD · Roman military writer
author.bio: Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus was a writer of the Later Roman Empire whose Epitoma rei militaris (also known as De re militari) is the only intact ancient manual of Roman military institutions. From it descends the famous adage Si vis pacem, para bellum — Vegetius’s own words were “Igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum” (“therefore let him who desires peace prepare for war”). That maxim, not anything by Sun Tzu, is the true ancestor of the popular quote.

misattribution.heading: How Sun Tzu got the credit
misattribution.intro: A clever, symmetrical war-and-peace line is exactly the kind of aphorism that drifts toward a famous strategist. Here the drift is documented.

items.why: The line does not appear in The Art of War. Wikiquote lists it under Sun Tzu’s Misattributed quotations ↗, explaining it is merely “sometimes erroneously prepended to the opening line ‘The art of war is of vital importance to the State.’”
The first half restates Si vis pacem, para bellum (“if you want peace, prepare for war”), whose documented origin is Vegetius’s De re militari ↗ — a Roman, not a Chinese, source.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: an anonymous modern saying that reverses a two-thousand-year-old Roman maxim, later pinned on Sun Tzu. Its earliest traced Google Books appearance is 1920, with no author named ↗.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Sun Tzu is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: any crisp aphorism about war, strategy or peace can be draped over his name and few readers will question it. The symmetry of this particular line — peace mirrored against war, war against peace — makes it feel ancient and Eastern, even though it is neither.

In reality the sentiment is Roman. Vegetius’s Si vis pacem, para bellum gave the West its enduring “prepare for war to keep the peace” maxim; the tidy “in war prepare for peace” counterpart is a modern rhetorical flourish that no primary text supports.
context.pull: An anonymous modern reversal of a Roman maxim — not a sentence Sun Tzu ever wrote.
